newsitem.title: CHINA: HK legislature dubbed rubber stamp, dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: HK legislature dubbed rubber stamp, dictatorship.

text.p: Shouts of "dictatorship" and "rubber stamp" marked the opening of Hong Kong's China-appointed legislature on Wednesday after the new government tried to rush through laws curbing trade unions and immigration.
Meanwhile, Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa got red carpet treatment and a pledge of non-interference as he inspected the Chinese garrison troops for the first time.
Activists from pro-democracy groups demonstrated outside the old colonial legislature building in central Hong Kong in a "day of mourning" for what they called "the death of democracy".
Others marched to Tung's office to denounce his bid to have the legislature "rubber-stamp" a bill suspending labour laws that beefed up workers' rights in the twilight of British rule.
Britain handed Hong Kong back to Beijing as a special Chinese region on July 1 after 156 years of colonial rule.
The capitalist way of life of its 6.4 million people is supposed to stay unchanged but the Tung government is already cutting back on democracy and civil rights.

Half of the 60-member pre-handover legislature have been thrown out of their seats. The assembly was disbanded last week and replaced by the 60-member appointed Provisional Legislature that held its first full-fledged session on Wednesday.

The government urged the chamber to ram through a law that would allow it to deport hundreds of illegal child immigrants from the Chinese mainland and suspend the labour laws -- without the traditional scrutiny and house committee processes.
The move has whipped up a whirlwind of polemics.

"We strongly condemn the government declaration. If this declaration is put into effect then the future of democracy is brought into question," said Bill Jordan, leader of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Trade Unions.
Activists from the Democratic Party and the Frontier group, angry labourers and 10 ousted legislators donned black headbands and played funeral music outside the legislature.
"Oppose the provisional legislature" and "A step back for democracy", they shouted.
They held up five rice bowls representing the rights of the workers. A note attached to the bowls read "collective bargaining power, no discrimination against trade unions".
Other demonstrators gathered around labour leader and ousted legislator Lee Cheuk-yan who declared a 120-hour hunger strike at the busy Star Ferry commuter pier.
About 40 protesters marched to Tung's office shouting "Oppose the puppet dictatorship" and handed in a protest note.
"The move shows that the legislative system of Hong Kong has completely collapsed. The legislature is only a rubber stamp which will follow the wish of the government," the letter said.

In a more positive sign, Tung addressed a world Lutheran congress and pledged to protect religious rights, prompting Lutheran leader Ishmael Noko to say: "I think there is a future for religious freedom."
And the head of the People's Liberation Army garrison, Major-General Liu Zhenwu, told Tung the army would not meddle.
"We will not interfere in the internal affairs of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR)," Liu said.
"We will not create troubles for the Hong Kong government. We will respect Hong Kong's way of life and the rule of law."
But the mood among Hong Kong democrats is sour.
"I feel very angry that the provisional legislature has no basis in law but now it is Hong Kong's law-making body," said former pro-democracy legislator Szeto Wah.
"Also, the laws we enacted before June 30 will be struck down. That will harm labour rights," Szeto said.

"We are wearing this black headband to signify a day of mourning for democracy. The provisional legislature meeting here is replacing an elected legislature, and this necessitates a day of mourning," said Democratic Party spokesman Cheung Yin-tin.
"The government is totally unchecked...This will make the government more authoritarian," said ex-legislator Yeung Sum.

One notable protest absentee was Democratic Party leader Martin Lee, who says he is not going near the legislative assembly building again until he wins back his seat -- possibly next May if new elections are held.
